title: The Ampersand and the hinge
instruction: Use the ampersand once per composition to join a commitment to what it produces.
intro: The ampersand is the hinge of the brand. It joins an oath, the commitment a person or an office makes, to the action that keeps it, and in our headlines it joins a rule to its result. Ampersand B is our own drawing: one pen path that crosses itself at the waist, with a beak at the top right and a tail that lands on the baseline.

This chapter covers B drawn alone and the four places the hinge appears: the hinge headline, the hinge divider, the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge. It ends with the tiles for avatars and the app icon, and the large crop for covers.

rules.title: Draw the ampersand from B’s master for its size.
rules.rule: B has three masters: the 16 px master for 16 to 23 px tall, the 24 px master for 24 to 47 px, and the display master from 48 px. Place the one whose range holds your height. A narrow drawing of B serves the condensed wordmark alone.

why.text: B’s strokes swell and thin at 1.74 to 1, so the glyph keeps its color beside the heavy capitals, and its waist crossing sits on the center line that the hinge diagram draws through its nodes. The small masters sit on the pixel grid: at 16 px, 66 percent of B’s ink pixels are solid, where the glyph in our brand guide’s fifth edition reached 48 percent.

correct.caption: B at true size on one baseline: the display master at 160 and 48 px, the 24 px master and the 16 px master. Below, enlarged four times, the 16 px master as the browser draws it in pixels, and its outline on the pixel grid.

failure.caption: Our fifth edition’s ampersand, placed from an old file. It is Lora Bold’s glyph, which anyone with Lora can type, and it has no beak.

rules.builders: The ampersand files draw in currentColor, so set color to the surface’s signature token. Our fifth edition’s OA_Amp_Master.svg holds the Lora glyph; retire it from your templates.

rules.title: Give each composition one ampersand moment.
rules.rule: A composition is one view: a screen, a card, a slide or a printed page. It carries one ampersand moment, a hinge headline, a freestanding B or a cropped B. The wordmark’s own ampersand and the hinge divider do not count.

why.text: The ampersand carries the brand’s idea, and a reader takes in one hinge at a time. With two or three on a card, each says less and the eye has no place to land.

correct.caption: A link card at 358 by 188 px, the size a phone feed shows it, with one hinge headline and the wordmark at its foot.

failure.caption: The same card with a cropped B in the corner and a second B beside the wordmark. Three ampersands compete for one glance.

specs.label: Moments
specs.value: A hinge headline, a freestanding B or a cropped B

specs.label: Not counted
specs.value: The wordmark’s ampersand and the hinge divider

rules.builders: When a template already holds a hinge headline, leave its ampersand slot out of every other layer.

rules.title: Join a rule to its result with a hinge headline, and give its ampersand the view’s working red.
rules.rule: A hinge headline joins two noun phrases with B, as in “The zoning code & the rent.” B takes the view’s working red, the one red each view may spend, unless an error or a step the reader can take now already holds it. Then B takes the headline’s ink. Rule 02.27 sets how to write one, and Rules 01.18 to 01.20 set when to use one.

why.text: The headline names a mechanism in five or six words, and the red ampersand marks the joint. Rule 05.3 ranks an error first and the step a reader can take now second, so on an Act piece with a red button the step keeps the red.

correct.caption: Three hinge headlines from Rule 02.27 at three sizes of the type scale, at true size: the title style at 56 px, the section style at 44 and H3 at 26. Each B comes from the master whose range holds that cap height.

failure.caption: An Act card with a red ampersand in its headline and a red button below it, two working reds in one view.

specs.value: Inter Tight 800, the headline’s tracking

rules.builders: Set B as an inline image of its master, joined to the second phrase with no-break spaces, so a line break falls at the hinge.

rules.title: Set a hinge divider between how a decision is made and what you can do about it.
rules.rule: The hinge divider centers B’s 24 px master on a 1 px line as wide as the text it divides, with 12 px of clear line on each side of B. Line and B take the surface’s ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. It is never red.

why.text: The divider marks the turn from how a decision is made to the step a reader can take, the same turn the ampersand makes in our name. In ink it stays quiet, and the view’s one working red stays free for the step itself.
why.basis: Rule 05.3, the red rule; Design judgment

correct.caption: A divider at true size in an article, between how a bill leaves committee and what a reader can do, and below it the divider on all four surfaces.

failure.caption: Our fifth edition’s divider, with a red ampersand, above a red button. The divider spends the view’s red, and two red marks compete for the step.

specs.value: B’s 24 px master at 24 px, at the center of the line

specs.label: Line
specs.value: 1 px, as wide as the text block it divides, in the same ink as B

specs.label: Above and below

rules.builders: Draw the line as two flexible halves with B between them, so B stays centered at any width. This guide draws the same divider between each rule and its correct use.

rules.title: Show the hinge diagram on its own, to explain the idea.
rules.rule: The hinge diagram draws OATH and ACTION on a line with four nodes, B in a ring between them, two solid arcs running clockwise, and UNDERSTAND and IMPACT beneath. Draw its lines solid, give it words alone, and keep it out of any view that holds the wordmark, the badge or a figure with a key. Where a page needs a break, use the divider.

why.text: The diagram teaches the brand’s idea in one picture: a promise becomes action, and the result shapes the next promise. Its arcs are solid because our systems atlas draws a hypothesis as a dotted line and a plausible link as a dashed one. It carries words alone, with no ID, sign, grade, delay or count, so no reader takes it for one of the atlas’s loops.

correct.caption: The display master at 600 px on Newsprint, and the compact master at 280 px on Newsprint and on Charcoal.

failure.caption: The diagram with dashed arcs and a dashed ring, as an early mockup drew it. In the atlas’s key a dashed line means a plausible link, so the brand’s own idea reads as unproven.

rules.title: Use the hinge-circle badge only to close a piece, on a back cover or at events.
rules.rule: The badge is B inside the hinge diagram’s ring, with no words. It ends an article or a report and marks event materials. Keep it off anything about a candidate or a ballot measure, where a seal-like mark could read as an endorsement. Keep it away from avatars, favicons and any view with the wordmark or the hinge diagram, and add no words or dates to it.

why.text: A ring of words and a founding date turn a badge into a seal, and our fifth edition put the reason plainly: “Seals imply an authority we do not claim.” With no words on it, the badge marks where a piece ends and claims nothing more.

correct.caption: The badge at true size as the end mark after an article’s last sentence, 16 px, and on the back of a 4 by 6 in event card, 96 px.

failure.caption: The badge turned into a seal with a ring of words. It claims an authority Oath & Action does not hold.

rules.builders: Set the end mark inline after the last word, with a no-break space before it, at the body text’s cap height or the 16 px master, whichever is larger.

rules.title: Put B on a Charcoal tile for avatars and the app icon.
rules.rule: Social avatars and the app icon show B alone on a Charcoal tile, a circle for avatars and a square for the app icon. The platform prints the account name beside an avatar, so the mark can be the ampersand alone. Favicons use B’s 16 px master with no tile.

why.text: A feed often draws an avatar at 32 to 48 px. B’s 24 px master still reads there, where any lettered mark would set its capitals under the 14 px floor. Charcoal is the default tile because it holds Pillar Red at 4.49 to 1, the strongest red of any approved surface, and stays visible on light and dark app themes.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11; Design judgment for the feed sizes

correct.caption: Avatars and the app icon at true size: B on a Charcoal circle at 180, 64 and 32 px and on a Charcoal square at 180 and 64 px; the Newsprint, Prussian and one-color tiles; and the favicon on a light and a dark browser tab.

failure.caption: A Newsprint circle in a white feed with no keyline. Its edge measures 1.41 to 1 against the page, so the tile fades and B floats.

rules.title: Crop a large B off the bottom-right corner only.
rules.rule: On a cover or a section opener, a large B may run off the bottom-right corner with 25 to 40 percent of its ink outside the frame. What stays inside reads as one letter, with no stroke cut off alone at the edge. It takes the surface’s ink, stays clear of the text, and never enters the top-left corner where reading starts.

why.text: Readers start at the top left, so a crop there sits in the way of the title. At the bottom right it frames the page and points to the turn. Rule 05.3 gives red no job for a crop, so it takes the surface’s ink, as the divider does.

correct.caption: A half-letter report cover at true size, 5.5 by 8.5 in, with B cropped off the bottom-right corner.

failure.caption: The crop moved up behind the title. The title’s letters cross B’s strokes and lose their edge.

specs.label: Outside the frame

specs.label: Inside the frame
specs.value: One piece: no stroke or fragment cut off from the letter at the trim

specs.label: Color

rules.builders: Place the display master in a frame with its overflow hidden, and move it until 25 to 40 percent of its ink sits outside and every part left inside the trim joins the rest of the letter, with no fragment alone at the edge.

sources: Oath & Action Brand Guide, fifth edition, chapter 04 The Ampersand, “Seal and emboss”. Quoted in Rule 04.6.
